title: Gratitude for everything
tomorrow: Amira's packing. from up here, which way does everything face?

segments.voice: Yesterday, what has changed: be glad at the gift, and keep your eyes on the road ahead. Who I am now. Today, what to do with the gladness.
screen: `WHO I AM NOW.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH THE GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: A living room with the furniture pushed back. Cushions on the floor, a tray of tea going cold, cousins with copies of the Qur'an open on their knees. For days the family has been reading it through, each person taking a part, and tonight the youngest, a seven-year-old, reads the very last surah, an-Nas, in a careful voice. Then it's done. The whole book. Someone exhales. And the grandmother, still healing from knee surgery, can't get down to the floor. So she leans forward from her chair as far as the knee allows, and bows her forehead to her open hands.
screen: `CUSHIONS, COLD TEA, OPEN BOOKS.` → `THE LAST SURAH.` → `A FOREHEAD BOWED TO OPEN HANDS.`

segments.voice: What she's doing has a name: sujud al-shukr, the prostration of thanks. A hadith in Abu Dawud says that when something came to the Prophet ﷺ that made him glad, he would fall down in prostration, thanking God. Not a speech. A body bending low. And when the knee won't bend, the tradition bends instead: the Prophet told a sick man to pray standing if he could, sitting if he couldn't, and on his side if he couldn't sit. Gratitude goes as low as the body allows. The words that go with it are the first words of the Fatiha: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Alhamdulillah. All praise. Here's the surprising part, worth telling a friend tonight. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet said the believer's whole affair is a wonder, because all of it is good: when something good comes, they give thanks, and that is good for them; when harm comes, they're patient, and that is good for them too. Gratitude for everything doesn't mean pretending the surgery didn't hurt, or the semester wasn't hard. It means the whole journey, the hard parts included, can end with a forehead lowered. Notice the senses of it: the cool of the floor, the smell of the carpet, the blood rushing to your face, your own breath close in your ears. Thanks you can feel.
screen: `SUJUD AL-SHUKR: THE BOW OF THANKS.` · `AS LOW AS THE BODY ALLOWS.` · `ALL OF IT IS GOOD.` · `THANKS YOU CAN FEEL.` · then, large: `ALL PRAISE.`

segments.voice: If you can, kneel and lower your forehead to the floor; if not, bow your head to your open hands from where you sit. Feel the floor or your palms against your forehead, and say alhamdulillah, or simply thank you, once for something good on this journey and once for something hard. Stay low until the time is up.
screen: `FOREHEAD TO THE FLOOR, OR TO YOUR HANDS.` · `ONCE FOR THE GOOD.` · `ONCE FOR THE HARD.`

segments.voice: Gratitude for everything: alhamdulillah for the whole journey, the good as thanks, the hard as patience.
Hold onto this: all praise, said with your whole body, as low as it will go. Thirteen of fifteen.

screen: `DAY 1789 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 13 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: FROM UP HERE, WHICH WAY DOES EVERYTHING FACE?`

howItsDone: When good news comes, many Muslims make a single prostration of thanks, sujud al-shukr, saying alhamdulillah; families often finish a khatm together with du'a and sweets.

chat.says: WE FINISHED THE KHATM. dadi wants to do sujud but can't kneel yet. is bowing from her chair ok?
options: Yes. The sick may pray sitting; she bows as low as the knee allows.
No. Sujud only counts with the forehead right on the ground.

chat.meaning: The Prophet told a sick man to pray sitting if he couldn't stand (Bukhari 1117). Gratitude bends as low as the body allows.

sujud al-shukr.meaning: a prostration of thanks when good news comes

an-Nas.meaning: 'mankind': the last surah of the Qur'an

Abu Dawud.meaning: a major collection of hadith, by Imam Abu Dawud

sources.quoted: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 2774 (the Prophet prostrated in thanks when something pleasing came to him)
Sahih Muslim 2999 (the believer's affair: thanks in good, patience in harm)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (pray standing; if not, sitting; if not, on your side)

notes: Bukhari 1117 concerns the obligatory prayer of a sick man; applying it to sujud al-shukr from a chair is by extension. Whether sujud al-shukr needs wudu and other conditions differs between schools; the script doesn't rule on it. Confirm.
Abu Dawud 2774 and Muslim 2999 paraphrased; confirm numbering.
